summary: Adds incremental zone transfer to DNS, so a secondary server can fetch only what changed in a zone instead of copying the whole thing. This saves bandwidth and time when large zones change in small ways.

eli5.summary: Instead of copying a whole book every time one page changes, you only get the changed pages. That is much faster than starting over.

questions: how to transfer only changes in a dns zone
how does incremental zone transfer work in dns
what is the ixfr query type number
subtitle: How a secondary DNS server can fetch only the changes to a zone instead of copying the whole thing.

tldr.problem: The full zone transfer (AXFR) copies an entire zone even when only a small part changed, which wastes effort when changes need to propagate quickly.
tldr.mechanism: A secondary sends an IXFR query carrying the SOA serial of its copy. The server replies with the sequence of deletions and additions that bring that version up to date, or falls back to a full transfer.
tldr.outcome: Servers keep a limited history of differences and may purge it, so IXFR is an optimization with a safe fallback. RFC 1995 is a Proposed Standard, updates RFC 1035 and is itself updated by RFC 9103.

today: RFC 1995 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1035 and is itself updated by RFC 9103; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Incremental Transfer
sections.content:
Changes to a DNS database need to propagate quickly. The NOTIFY extension (RFC 1996) cuts latency by actively telling servers that a zone changed. But the existing full zone transfer, AXFR, sends the entire zone file, which is inefficient when only a small part changed.

IXFR transfers only the changed portions. The RFC names the roles: a secondary name server that requests IXFR is an IXFR client, and a primary or secondary server that responds is an IXFR server.
sections.eli5: Copying a whole phone book because one number changed is a waste. IXFR sends just the changed lines.

sections.title: How the Exchange Works
sections.content:
A client that thinks it needs new data, typically because the SOA refresh timer fired or a NOTIFY arrived, sends an IXFR message containing the SOA serial number of its possibly outdated copy. The server keeps the newest version of the zone plus the differences between it and several older versions, and sends only the differences needed to bring the client current. It may instead send the entire zone, as in a normal AXFR.

If the query carries the same or a newer serial than the server's, the reply is a single SOA record of the server's current version, just as in AXFR.

The query may use UDP or TCP. Over UDP the server may reply in UDP only if the whole response fits in one DNS packet; otherwise it answers with a single SOA record to tell the client to retry over TCP. So a client should first try IXFR over UDP. If the server does not recognize the query type, the client should try AXFR, preceded by a UDP SOA query. If the answer is a single packet with the whole new zone, or the server has nothing newer, it is done; otherwise it should try a TCP IXFR.

For integrity, servers should use UDP checksums on all UDP responses, and a cautious client that gets a UDP packet with a zero checksum should ignore it and try TCP. A server should also save a new zone version to stable storage before using it to answer IXFR or AXFR queries, so a crash cannot leave secondaries holding data the server no longer has. The IXFR query type value assigned by IANA is 251.
sections.eli5: You tell the server which edition of the book you have. It sends the changes since then, or the whole book if that is easier, or tells you to ask again in a bigger envelope if the changes do not fit on a postcard.

sections.title: Query and Response Format
sections.content:
An IXFR query has the format of a normal DNS query, with query type IXFR and the authority section holding the SOA record of the client's version of the zone.

If incremental transfer is not available, the entire zone comes back: the first and last RR are the zone's SOA, exactly like an AXFR response.

If it is available, the response holds one or more difference sequences, preceded and followed by a copy of the server's current SOA. Each sequence is one update, one SOA serial change, made of deleted RRs and added RRs. The first deleted RR is the older SOA and the first added RR is the newer SOA. Changing an RR is done by deleting the original and adding the modified one. Sequences go oldest first, so together they are the history from the client's version up to the current one. RRs may be partial: if one of several RRs of the same type changes, only that one is sent.

An incremental response therefore starts with two SOA RRs: the server's current SOA, then the SOA of the client's version about to be replaced. The client should replace its old version only after all differences have been processed successfully.
sections.eli5: The answer is a list of edits, oldest first: take these lines out, put these lines in. You only swap your copy once every edit has been applied without a problem.

sections.title: Purging and Condensing History
sections.content:
A server cannot be required to keep every old version and may delete them at any time. The trade-off is storage against how often IXFR can be used. Old versions should be purged if an IXFR response would be longer than an AXFR response, which keeps storage to at most twice the current zone. Information older than the SOA expire period may also be purged.

A server may also condense several difference sequences into one, dropping intermediate versions. This helps when many versions are generated and few matter, such as an address that changes once a minute to balance load between ftp servers. It is less useful if a client talks to two servers that condense differently: the version received from server A may be unknown to server B, which then cannot give an incremental answer and a full transfer is needed. Clients cannot tell from a response whether it was condensed.

For interoperability, servers should not return an error for an unknown version number and should instead attempt a full zone transfer.
sections.eli5: The server cannot keep every old edition forever. If keeping the edits would take more room than the whole book, it throws them away and just sends the whole book next time.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC uses the zone JAIN.AD.JP. with three generations, serial 1 to 3. From serial 1 to 2, NEZU.JAIN.AD.JP. is removed and JAIN-BB.JAIN.AD.JP. is added. From 2 to 3, one address of JAIN-BB changes from 133.69.136.4 to 133.69.136.3.

A client at serial 1 sends an IXFR query. The server could reply with a full zone transfer, with the incremental message of two difference sequences, with a condensed single sequence going from 1 to 3, or, on UDP overflow, with just the serial 3 SOA record.
sections.eli5: The same change can be sent as the whole list, as each edit in order, as one combined edit, or as a note saying to ask again another way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC makes no attempt to fix the security problems of DNS. It states that it is believed to introduce no additional security problems to the existing DNS protocol.
sections.eli5: This memo does not try to make DNS safer, and it does not think it makes DNS less safe either.
